name: Hydrogen
summary: Hydrogen is the lightest element and by far the most common one in the universe, where it is the fuel that powers stars. On Earth it is mostly locked up in water and in the molecules of living things.
fact: About three quarters of the ordinary matter in the universe, measured by mass, is hydrogen, almost all of it formed shortly after the Big Bang.

name: Helium
summary: Helium is a colorless, very light gas that does not react with other elements. It matters because liquid helium is cold enough to chill the powerful magnets inside hospital MRI scanners, and the gas lifts balloons and airships.
fact: Helium was first detected in sunlight during an 1868 solar eclipse, well before chemists managed to collect any of it on Earth.

name: Lithium
summary: Lithium is a soft, silvery metal so light that it floats on water, fizzing as it reacts. It matters because lithium-based batteries store the energy that runs phones, laptops, and electric cars.
fact: Along with hydrogen and helium, a tiny amount of lithium was made in the first minutes after the Big Bang, long before any stars existed.

name: Beryllium
summary: Beryllium is a hard, gray metal that is unusually light and stiff. It matters in aerospace and science, where it is used for precision parts, although its dust is toxic and must be handled with great care.
fact: Emeralds and aquamarines are both varieties of beryl, a mineral containing beryllium, with traces of other elements giving each gemstone its color.

name: Boron
summary: Boron is a hard, dark element whose behavior sits between that of metals and nonmetals. It matters because its compounds make glass that survives sudden temperature changes, and plants need small amounts of it to grow.
fact: Boron carbide, a compound of boron and carbon, is one of the hardest materials known and is used in body armor.

name: Carbon
summary: Carbon is the element at the heart of all known life, because its atoms can link into long chains and rings. It also forms coal, graphite, and diamond, and the carbon dioxide that affects Earth's climate.
fact: Sparkling diamond and the soft graphite in a pencil are both pure carbon, differing only in the way their atoms are arranged.

name: Nitrogen
summary: Nitrogen is a colorless gas that makes up most of the air you breathe. It matters because every protein and every strand of DNA contains it, so all living things need it to grow.
fact: Although nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of the air, most living things cannot use it until bacteria or lightning turn it into other compounds.

name: Oxygen
summary: Oxygen is the gas that most living things need to release energy from food, and it makes up about a fifth of the air. It also combines with most other elements, which is what happens in burning and rusting.
fact: Liquid oxygen is pale blue and magnetic enough to be held between the poles of a strong magnet.

name: Fluorine
summary: Fluorine is a pale yellow, poisonous gas that reacts with almost everything it touches. It matters because its compounds, called fluorides, strengthen tooth enamel, and others are used to make nonstick coatings for cookware.
fact: Fluorine is so dangerous to handle that several chemists were injured or killed trying to isolate it before Henri Moissan succeeded in 1886.

name: Neon
summary: Neon is a colorless gas that does not react with other elements. It matters because it glows a brilliant reddish orange when electricity passes through it, which made bright advertising signs possible.
fact: Pure neon glows only reddish orange, so many so-called neon signs in other colors actually use different gases or coated glass tubes.

name: Sodium
summary: Sodium is a soft, silvery metal that reacts violently with water. It matters because, joined with chlorine, it forms table salt, and your nerves and muscles need sodium to send their signals.
fact: Sodium metal is soft enough to slice with a butter knife and is stored under oil to keep it away from air and moisture.

name: Magnesium
summary: Magnesium is a light, silvery metal that burns with a dazzling white flame. It matters because it makes strong, lightweight alloys for cars and aircraft, and your body needs it for healthy muscles and bones.
fact: Every molecule of chlorophyll, the green pigment plants use to capture sunlight, has a single magnesium atom at its center.

name: Aluminum
summary: Aluminum is a light, silvery metal that resists corrosion because a thin oxide layer protects its surface. It matters because it is strong for its weight, which makes it ideal for aircraft, drink cans, and foil.
fact: Before cheap electricity, aluminum was so hard to extract that it was treated as a precious metal, even though it is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust.

name: Silicon
summary: Silicon is a hard, gray, shiny element that behaves partly like a metal and partly like a nonmetal. It matters because computer chips and most solar cells are built on thin slices of very pure silicon.
fact: Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust after oxygen, and together the two make up sand and most common rocks.

name: Phosphorus
summary: Phosphorus is a reactive nonmetal that comes in several forms, including white and red. It matters because it is part of DNA, bones, and teeth, and farmers rely on phosphate fertilizers to grow crops.
fact: Phosphorus was discovered in 1669 by Hennig Brand, an alchemist who boiled down large amounts of urine while searching for a way to make gold.

name: Sulfur
summary: Sulfur is a bright yellow, brittle nonmetal often found near volcanoes and hot springs. It matters because it is made into sulfuric acid, one of the most widely produced industrial chemicals in the world.
fact: Pure sulfur has no smell, and the rotten-egg stink people blame on it actually comes from hydrogen sulfide, a compound of sulfur and hydrogen.

name: Chlorine
summary: Chlorine is a yellow-green, poisonous gas with a sharp, choking smell. It matters because small amounts kill germs in drinking water and swimming pools, and it is one of the two elements in table salt.
fact: Chlorine gas was used as a weapon in the First World War, yet adding chlorine to drinking water has saved enormous numbers of lives.

name: Argon
summary: Argon is a colorless, odorless gas that almost never reacts with anything. It matters because this unreactive nature makes it an ideal protective blanket for welding metals and for filling light bulbs.
fact: Argon is the third most common gas in dry air, making up nearly one percent of every breath you take.

name: Potassium
summary: Potassium is a soft, silvery metal that reacts so fiercely with water that it catches fire. It matters because your nerves and muscles, including your heart, need potassium to work, and plants need it to grow.
fact: A tiny fraction of all potassium is naturally radioactive, so bananas and even your own body give off a very small, harmless amount of radiation.

name: Calcium
summary: Calcium is a silvery metal that is never found pure in nature because it reacts with air and water. It matters because its compounds build strong bones and teeth and are a main ingredient of cement.
fact: Marble, limestone, eggshells, seashells, and pearls are all made mainly of the same compound, calcium carbonate.

name: Scandium
summary: Scandium is a soft, silvery metal that is spread thinly through Earth's crust and is costly to extract. It matters because adding a little to aluminum makes alloys that are both strong and light.
fact: Dmitri Mendeleev predicted this element and its properties, calling it eka-boron, several years before it was discovered in Sweden in 1879.

name: Titanium
summary: Titanium is a silvery metal that is about as strong as steel but much lighter, and it resists corrosion very well. It matters for aircraft, spacecraft, and medical implants, because the human body accepts it readily.
fact: Most titanium is not used as a metal at all but as titanium dioxide, the brilliant white pigment in paint, sunscreen, and toothpaste.

name: Vanadium
summary: Vanadium is a hard, silvery-gray metal that is mostly used in small amounts mixed into steel. It matters because even a little makes steel much tougher and more resistant to shock and wear.
fact: Vanadium was named after Vanadis, another name for the Norse goddess Freyja, because its compounds come in so many beautiful colors.

name: Chromium
summary: Chromium is a hard, silvery metal that can be polished to a mirror-like shine. It matters because adding it to steel creates stainless steel, which resists rust and stains in kitchens, hospitals, and factories.
fact: Tiny traces of chromium are what give rubies their deep red color and emeralds their rich green color.

name: Manganese
summary: Manganese is a hard, brittle, grayish metal that is rarely used on its own. It matters because nearly all steel contains some manganese, which makes the steel stronger and easier to shape.
fact: Potato-sized lumps rich in manganese, called nodules, lie scattered across large areas of the deep ocean floor, having grown extremely slowly over millions of years.

name: Iron
summary: Iron is a strong, grayish metal and the main ingredient of steel, which is used in buildings, bridges, cars, and tools. It also matters inside your body, where iron in your blood helps carry oxygen.
fact: Earth's core is made mostly of iron, and the swirling motion of its liquid outer layer generates the planet's magnetic field.

name: Cobalt
summary: Cobalt is a hard, bluish-gray metal that can be magnetized. It matters because it is used in many rechargeable batteries and in tough alloys that survive the heat inside jet engines.
fact: Cobalt's name comes from kobold, a German word for a goblin, because miners long ago blamed mischievous spirits for its troublesome ores.

name: Nickel
summary: Nickel is a silvery-white metal that resists corrosion and can be magnetized. It matters because it is a key ingredient of stainless steel and is also used in coins and rechargeable batteries.
fact: The US five-cent coin known as a nickel is actually three quarters copper and only one quarter nickel.

name: Copper
summary: Copper is a reddish-orange metal that conducts electricity and heat extremely well. It matters because most electrical wiring is made of it, and people have been shaping it into tools for thousands of years.
fact: The Statue of Liberty is covered in copper sheets, which slowly turned from reddish brown to green as the metal reacted with the air.

name: Zinc
summary: Zinc is a bluish-white metal that protects other metals from rusting. It matters because coating steel with zinc, called galvanizing, makes it last far longer, and your body needs zinc to stay healthy.
fact: US pennies made since 1983 are almost entirely zinc, with just a thin coating of copper on the outside.

name: Gallium
summary: Gallium is a soft, silvery metal that is not found pure in nature. It matters because its compounds are used in LEDs, lasers, and the fast electronic chips inside mobile phones.
fact: Gallium melts at about 30 degrees Celsius, so a solid piece will slowly turn to liquid in the palm of your hand.

name: Germanium
summary: Germanium is a hard, grayish-white element that is a semiconductor, meaning it conducts electricity better than an insulator but worse than a metal. It matters because it is used in fiber-optic cables and in lenses for infrared cameras.
fact: The very first transistor, built at Bell Labs in 1947, used germanium rather than the silicon that dominates electronics today.

name: Arsenic
summary: Arsenic is a gray, brittle element best known as a notorious poison. It still matters today because small amounts are used in electronics, and natural arsenic in groundwater is a serious health problem in some countries.
fact: In the 1800s a fashionable green pigment containing arsenic was used in wallpaper and clothing, sometimes making people ill.

name: Selenium
summary: Selenium is a nonmetal that conducts electricity better when light shines on it. It matters because your body needs tiny amounts of it to stay healthy, although too much is poisonous.
fact: Selenium was named after Selene, the Greek goddess of the Moon, to pair it with tellurium, which had been named after the Earth.

name: Bromine
summary: Bromine is a dark reddish-brown liquid that gives off choking, orange-brown fumes. It matters because its compounds are used to make materials harder to set alight and to keep water free of germs.
fact: Bromine is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature, and its name comes from a Greek word meaning stench.

name: Krypton
summary: Krypton is a colorless, odorless gas found in tiny traces in the air. It matters because it is used in some bright lamps and lasers, and it helps insulate energy-saving windows.
fact: From 1960 to 1983 the meter was officially defined using the wavelength of orange-red light given off by krypton atoms.

name: Rubidium
summary: Rubidium is a very soft, silvery metal that reacts violently with water and can catch fire in air. It matters mostly in science and technology, where it is used in very accurate clocks.
fact: Rubidium's name comes from the Latin for deep red, after the red lines scientists saw when they first examined its light.

name: Strontium
summary: Strontium is a soft, silvery metal that quickly turns yellowish in air. It matters because its compounds produce the brilliant red colors in fireworks and flares, and others make long-lasting glow-in-the-dark materials.
fact: Strontium is named after Strontian, a village in Scotland where the mineral containing it was first found.

name: Yttrium
summary: Yttrium is a silvery metal usually grouped with the rare earth elements. It matters because its compounds are used in white LEDs, lasers, and materials that conduct electricity without resistance when cooled.
fact: Four elements, yttrium, ytterbium, terbium, and erbium, are all named after the same small Swedish village, Ytterby.

name: Zirconium
summary: Zirconium is a strong, silvery-gray metal that resists corrosion extremely well. It matters in nuclear power stations, where it is used to wrap the fuel because it lets neutrons pass through easily.
fact: Cubic zirconia, a sparkling crystal form of zirconium dioxide, is widely used as an inexpensive stand-in for diamond in jewelry.

name: Niobium
summary: Niobium is a soft, gray metal that makes steel much stronger when a small amount is added. It matters because niobium alloys can carry electricity with no resistance at very low temperatures, making powerful magnets possible.
fact: Niobium is named after Niobe, daughter of Tantalus in Greek myth, because it is so similar to the element tantalum.

name: Molybdenum
summary: Molybdenum is a silvery metal with a very high melting point. It matters because adding it to steel makes the steel stronger and more resistant to heat and corrosion, which suits it to tools and engine parts.
fact: Many of the bacteria that turn nitrogen from the air into food for plants depend on an enzyme that contains molybdenum.

name: Technetium
summary: Technetium is a silvery, radioactive metal with no stable forms, so almost none exists naturally on Earth. It matters in hospitals, where a short-lived form helps doctors take images of organs and bones.
fact: Technetium was the first element to be made artificially, and its name comes from a Greek word meaning artificial.

name: Ruthenium
summary: Ruthenium is a rare, hard, silvery-white metal belonging to the platinum family. It matters because small amounts harden other precious metals and help make durable electrical contacts and computer hard disks.
fact: Ruthenium is named after Ruthenia, a Latin name for Russia, where the ore it was discovered in had been mined.

name: Rhodium
summary: Rhodium is a rare, silvery-white metal that is very hard and highly reflective. It matters because it is used in car exhaust systems to turn harmful gases into less harmful ones.
fact: Rhodium is one of the rarest and most expensive precious metals, and at times it has cost many times more than gold.

name: Palladium
summary: Palladium is a rare, silvery-white precious metal closely related to platinum. It matters because most of it goes into catalytic converters, which clean up the exhaust fumes from gasoline-powered cars.
fact: Palladium can soak up hydrogen like a sponge, absorbing hundreds of times its own volume of the gas.

name: Silver
summary: Silver is a shiny, white precious metal that people have made into jewelry and coins for thousands of years. It matters in technology too, because it is used in solar panels and electronics.
fact: Silver conducts both electricity and heat better than any other metal, beating even copper, though it is too costly for ordinary wiring.

name: Cadmium
summary: Cadmium is a soft, bluish-white metal that is toxic to people and wildlife. It matters because it has been widely used in rechargeable batteries and pigments, so it must be handled and recycled carefully.
fact: Cadmium compounds give artists some of their brightest yellow, orange, and red paints, which have been popular since the 1800s.

name: Indium
summary: Indium is a very soft, silvery metal that can be scratched with a fingernail. It matters because a transparent compound containing indium conducts electricity, which is what makes touchscreens and flat-panel displays work.
fact: Indium is named after the bright indigo-blue line seen in its light spectrum, not after the country of India.

name: Tin
summary: Tin is a soft, silvery metal that resists corrosion. It matters because a thin coating of it protects steel food cans, and mixing it with copper makes bronze, one of the earliest alloys people used.
fact: In very cold conditions tin can slowly crumble into a gray powder, a change nicknamed tin pest.

name: Antimony
summary: Antimony is a brittle, silvery-gray element with properties between those of metals and nonmetals. It matters because its compounds make plastics and fabrics harder to burn, and it hardens the lead used in batteries.
fact: Antimony's symbol Sb comes from stibium, its Latin name, and its dark mineral stibnite was ground into eye makeup in parts of the ancient world.

name: Tellurium
summary: Tellurium is a brittle, silvery-white element that is one of the rarest in Earth's crust. It matters because it is used in some solar panels and in alloys that are easier to cut and shape.
fact: People who absorb even tiny amounts of tellurium develop breath that smells strongly of garlic, an effect that can linger for weeks.

name: Iodine
summary: Iodine is a dark, shiny solid that turns into a violet vapor when warmed. It matters because your thyroid gland needs it to make hormones that control growth and how your body uses energy.
fact: Iodine was discovered in 1811 by Bernard Courtois, who noticed purple vapor rising from seaweed ash he was treating with acid.

name: Xenon
summary: Xenon is a heavy, colorless gas present in the air in very small traces. It matters because it gives a brilliant white light in lamps and is used to propel some spacecraft.
fact: Xenon was thought to be completely unreactive until 1962, when Neil Bartlett used it to make the first noble gas compound.

name: Cesium
summary: Cesium is a soft, pale gold metal that melts just above room temperature and reacts explosively with water. It matters because clocks based on cesium atoms keep time accurately enough to set the world's official time.
fact: Since 1967 the second has been officially defined by counting a particular vibration of cesium atoms that repeats more than nine billion times.

name: Barium
summary: Barium is a soft, silvery metal that reacts quickly with air and water, so it is never found pure in nature. It matters because one of its compounds shows up clearly on X-rays, helping doctors examine the digestive system.
fact: Barium compounds that dissolve in water are poisonous, yet barium sulfate is safe to swallow for X-rays because it does not dissolve in the body.

name: Lanthanum
summary: Lanthanum is a soft, silvery-white metal that gives its name to the lanthanide series of elements. It matters because it is used in camera lenses, oil refining, and the batteries of many hybrid cars.
fact: Lanthanum's name comes from a Greek word meaning to lie hidden, because it was found concealed inside a mineral of cerium.

name: Cerium
summary: Cerium is a soft, gray metal and the most abundant of the rare earth elements. It matters because its oxide is used to polish glass and to help clean up car exhaust fumes.
fact: The sparks from a cigarette lighter's flint come from an alloy rich in cerium, which sheds burning shavings when it is scratched.

name: Praseodymium
summary: Praseodymium is a soft, silvery rare earth metal that slowly develops a green coating in air. It matters because it helps make very strong magnets and special glass that protects the eyes of welders and glassblowers.
fact: Its name means green twin in Greek, because it was separated in 1885 from a material once believed to be a single element.

name: Neodymium
summary: Neodymium is a silvery rare earth metal used to make very strong permanent magnets. These magnets are found in headphones, electric car motors, and wind turbines, which makes the element important for modern technology.
fact: Glass colored with neodymium appears lilac in daylight but can look pale blue under fluorescent lamps, because it absorbs a narrow band of yellow light.

name: Promethium
summary: Promethium is a radioactive rare earth metal that is almost never found in nature. All of its forms decay away, so the tiny amounts that scientists use are made in nuclear reactors.
fact: Promethium is named after Prometheus, the figure in Greek myth who stole fire from the gods and gave it to humans.

name: Samarium
summary: Samarium is a silvery rare earth metal that helps make magnets which keep working at high temperatures. It is also good at absorbing neutrons, so it is useful inside nuclear reactors.
fact: Samarium takes its name from the mineral samarskite, which honors Vasili Samarsky-Bykhovets, a Russian mining official who gave scientists access to the mineral samples.

name: Europium
summary: Europium is a soft, silvery rare earth metal that reacts quickly with air and water. Its compounds glow brightly when energized, which makes the element valuable for producing red and blue light in screens and lamps.
fact: Europium is named after the continent of Europe, and its compounds that glow under ultraviolet light are used in security inks that help expose forged documents.

name: Gadolinium
summary: Gadolinium is a silvery rare earth metal with unusual magnetic properties. Doctors use its compounds to make MRI scans clearer, and it is excellent at absorbing neutrons inside nuclear reactors.
fact: Gadolinium is strongly magnetic like iron on a cool day, but it loses that strong magnetism when it is warmed to roughly room temperature.

name: Terbium
summary: Terbium is a soft, silvery rare earth metal whose compounds glow bright green. That green glow helps create the colors in screens and efficient lamps, and terbium also improves powerful magnets.
fact: Four elements, terbium, yttrium, erbium, and ytterbium, are all named after the same small Swedish village, Ytterby, where their minerals were first found.

name: Dysprosium
summary: Dysprosium is a bright, silvery rare earth metal that is added to powerful magnets. It helps those magnets keep their strength when they get hot, which matters in electric cars and wind turbines.
fact: Dysprosium's name comes from a Greek word meaning hard to get at, because its discoverer needed many repeated steps to separate it.

name: Holmium
summary: Holmium is a soft, silvery rare earth metal with remarkable magnetic strength. It is used in special magnets and in medical lasers that help surgeons cut tissue and break up kidney stones.
fact: Holmium gets its name from Holmia, the Latin name for Stockholm, the Swedish capital that lies close to where many rare earth minerals were found.

name: Erbium
summary: Erbium is a soft, silvery rare earth metal that gives glass a pink color. Tiny amounts inside optical fibers boost the light signals that carry internet data across long distances.
fact: Early chemists confused erbium with terbium so badly that the two names ended up swapped compared with how their discoverer first assigned them.

name: Thulium
summary: Thulium is a silvery rare earth metal that is among the scarcest of its family. A radioactive form of it gives off X-rays and has been used in portable X-ray devices that need no electricity supply.
fact: Thulium is named after Thule, an ancient name for a mysterious land in the far north that is often linked with Scandinavia.

name: Ytterbium
summary: Ytterbium is a soft, silvery rare earth metal that is fairly easy to bend and shape. It is used in powerful industrial lasers and in some of the most accurate atomic clocks ever built.
fact: Ytterbium's electrical resistance changes when it is squeezed very hard, so it has been used in gauges that measure the shock from explosions and earthquakes.

name: Lutetium
summary: Lutetium is a hard, dense, silvery metal that is the last member of the lanthanide series. It is difficult to separate from its neighbors, and it is used in medical scanners and cancer treatment.
fact: Lutetium is named after Lutetia, the Roman name for the settlement that grew into the city of Paris.

name: Hafnium
summary: Hafnium is a shiny, silvery metal that resists corrosion and absorbs neutrons very well. This makes it useful for controlling nuclear reactors, and its compounds help shrink the transistors inside computer chips.
fact: Hafnium is named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, where it was finally found hiding in minerals of zirconium, which it closely resembles.

name: Tantalum
summary: Tantalum is a hard, blue-gray metal that is extremely resistant to corrosion. It is used to make tiny capacitors for phones and computers, and the human body tolerates it well in implants.
fact: Tantalum is named after Tantalus from Greek myth, who stood in water he could never drink, because the metal's oxide would not take up acid.

name: Tungsten
summary: Tungsten is a very dense, gray metal with the highest melting point of all metals. Its strength at extreme heat makes it valuable for cutting tools, light bulb filaments, and rocket parts.
fact: Tungsten means heavy stone in Swedish, yet its symbol W comes from its other name, wolfram, which is still used in several languages.

name: Rhenium
summary: Rhenium is a rare, dense, silvery metal with an extremely high melting point. It is added to the alloys used in jet engine turbine blades so that they can survive intense heat.
fact: Rhenium is named after the Rhine river in Germany, and it was the last element with a stable form to be discovered.

name: Osmium
summary: Osmium is a hard, bluish-white metal that is one of the densest substances known. It is very rare, and it is mixed with other metals to make extremely hard-wearing parts.
fact: Osmium's name comes from the Greek word for smell, because its powder slowly forms a toxic compound in air that has a sharp odor.

name: Iridium
summary: Iridium is a hard, silvery-white metal that is among the most corrosion-resistant metals known. It is extremely rare in Earth's crust and is used where parts must survive great heat and wear.
fact: A thin layer of iridium-rich clay found around the world is key evidence that an asteroid struck Earth when the dinosaurs died out.

name: Platinum
summary: Platinum is a dense, silvery-white precious metal that does not tarnish. It is prized for jewelry, and it speeds up chemical reactions, which helps clean car exhaust and produce many useful chemicals.
fact: Spanish explorers in South America called platinum platina, meaning little silver, and at first considered it a nuisance mixed in with their gold.

name: Gold
summary: Gold is a soft, yellow precious metal that does not rust or tarnish. People have treasured it for thousands of years as jewelry and money, and it is also an excellent conductor in electronics.
fact: Gold can be hammered into sheets so thin that they become see-through, and its symbol Au comes from aurum, the Latin word for gold.

name: Mercury
summary: Mercury is a heavy, silvery metal that is liquid at room temperature. It was once common in thermometers, but it is poisonous, so many of its uses are now being phased out.
fact: Mercury is so dense that pieces of solid lead and even iron cannonballs will float on its surface instead of sinking.

name: Thallium
summary: Thallium is a soft, gray metal that is highly poisonous. It was once used in rat poison, and today small amounts are used in electronics, special glass, and medical heart scans.
fact: Thallium was discovered by the bright green line it gives off in a flame, and its name comes from a Greek word for a green shoot.

name: Lead
summary: Lead is a soft, heavy, gray metal that is easy to melt and shape. It is very useful in batteries and radiation shielding, but it is poisonous, so it has been removed from most paint and gasoline.
fact: The word plumbing and lead's symbol Pb both come from plumbum, the Latin name for lead, because Roman water pipes were made from it.

name: Bismuth
summary: Bismuth is a brittle, silvery metal with a faint pink tinge. It is far less toxic than neighbors such as lead, so it is used in medicines, cosmetics, and lead-free alloys.
fact: Bismuth crystals grown in a laboratory form staircase-like spirals coated in a thin oxide layer that shimmers with rainbow colors.

name: Polonium
summary: Polonium is a rare, intensely radioactive metal found in tiny traces in uranium ores. It gives off so much energy that a small sample heats itself, and it is extremely dangerous if swallowed or inhaled.
fact: Marie Curie named polonium after Poland, her homeland, which at the time did not exist as an independent country.

name: Astatine
summary: Astatine is an extremely rare radioactive element that forms in tiny traces as heavier elements decay. So little exists that nobody has ever seen a visible piece, and scientists study it mainly for possible cancer treatments.
fact: Astatine's name comes from the Greek word for unstable, which suits an element whose longest-lived form has a half-life of only about eight hours.

name: Radon
summary: Radon is a colorless, odorless radioactive gas that forms naturally as uranium in rocks and soil breaks down. It can seep into buildings and collect in basements, where breathing it for years raises lung cancer risk.
fact: Radon is the heaviest of the noble gases found in nature, and it is roughly eight times denser than the air around us.

name: Francium
summary: Francium is an extremely rare, highly radioactive metal that forms briefly in uranium ores. Its atoms break down so quickly that it has no practical uses and is studied only in tiny amounts.
fact: Francium was discovered by Marguerite Perey, a former assistant of Marie Curie, who named the new element after her home country, France.

name: Radium
summary: Radium is a silvery-white radioactive metal found in tiny amounts in uranium ores. It once made watch dials glow in the dark, until people learned how dangerous its radiation is.
fact: Factory workers known as the Radium Girls became seriously ill after licking their brushes to a point while painting glowing radium onto watch dials.

name: Actinium
summary: Actinium is a soft, silvery radioactive metal that glows pale blue in the dark. It is very rare in nature, and one form of it is being developed for targeted cancer treatments.
fact: Actinium gives its name to the actinides, the row of fifteen radioactive elements that starts with it and ends with lawrencium.

name: Thorium
summary: Thorium is a silvery, slightly radioactive metal that is more common in Earth's crust than uranium. It can be turned into nuclear fuel, so scientists are studying it as a possible future energy source.
fact: Thorium was named after Thor, the Norse god of thunder, by the Swedish chemist Berzelius, who first identified the element.

name: Protactinium
summary: Protactinium is a dense, silvery radioactive metal that is very rare and highly toxic. It has no everyday uses, but measuring it in ocean sediments helps scientists learn about past ocean currents.
fact: Protactinium's name means parent of actinium, because it slowly decays into actinium as it gives off radiation.

name: Uranium
summary: Uranium is a heavy, silvery radioactive metal found in rocks around the world. Splitting its atoms releases enormous energy, which powers the nuclear reactors that generate electricity in many countries.
fact: Uranium was named after the planet Uranus, which had been discovered only eight years before the element was identified in 1789.

name: Neptunium
summary: Neptunium is a silvery radioactive metal that is made inside nuclear reactors. It was the first element heavier than uranium to be produced, opening the way to many more artificial elements.
fact: Neptunium is named after the planet Neptune because it follows uranium in the table, just as Neptune follows Uranus in the solar system.

name: Plutonium
summary: Plutonium is a heavy, silvery radioactive metal made in nuclear reactors. It can release huge amounts of energy, so it is used in nuclear weapons, some reactors, and long-lasting power supplies for spacecraft.
fact: Plutonium was named after Pluto, continuing the planet pattern set by uranium and neptunium, back when Pluto was still counted as a planet.

name: Americium
summary: Americium is a silvery radioactive metal made in nuclear reactors. It is one of the few artificial elements found in ordinary homes, because tiny amounts are used in many smoke detectors.
fact: Americium was discovered during the Manhattan Project, and Glenn Seaborg first revealed it to the public while answering a question on a children's radio quiz show.

name: Curium
summary: Curium is a hard, silvery radioactive metal made in nuclear reactors. It is so radioactive that it glows in the dark, and it provides particles for instruments that study rocks on Mars.
fact: Curium is named after Marie and Pierre Curie, the married scientists who pioneered the study of radioactivity.

name: Berkelium
summary: Berkelium is a soft, silvery radioactive metal that is produced only in tiny amounts in special nuclear reactors. It has no everyday uses, but scientists use it as a target for making heavier elements.
fact: Berkelium is named after Berkeley, California, and a berkelium target was used to create the first atoms of tennessine.

name: Californium
summary: Californium is a silvery radioactive metal made in nuclear reactors. It gives off a strong stream of neutrons, which makes it valuable for starting reactors and for finding metals and oil underground.
fact: Californium is named after the state and university of California, and its price has been quoted at millions of dollars per gram.

name: Einsteinium
summary: Einsteinium is a soft, silvery radioactive metal that is made only in tiny amounts. It is too rare and short-lived for everyday uses, so it is studied purely for scientific research.
fact: Einsteinium was first found in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb test in 1952, and its discovery was kept secret for several years.

name: Fermium
summary: Fermium is a radioactive metal that has only ever been produced in amounts far too small to see. It has no uses outside research, where it helps scientists understand very heavy atoms.
fact: Fermium is named after Enrico Fermi, who led the team that built the first nuclear reactor, and it was first found in hydrogen bomb debris.

name: Mendelevium
summary: Mendelevium is a radioactive metal that can only be made in particle accelerators, in amounts far too small to see. It has no practical uses, but studying it teaches scientists about the heaviest elements.
fact: Mendelevium is named after Dmitri Mendeleev, the Russian chemist who created an early periodic table and left gaps for elements not yet discovered.

name: Nobelium
summary: Nobelium is a radioactive metal made only in extremely small quantities in particle accelerators. Its atoms break down quickly, so it has no practical uses and is studied only in specialized laboratories.
fact: Nobelium is named after Alfred Nobel, the Swedish inventor of dynamite whose fortune was used to found the Nobel Prizes.

name: Lawrencium
summary: Lawrencium is a radioactive metal that is the final member of the actinide series. It can only be made in extremely small quantities, so it is used purely for scientific research.
fact: Lawrencium is named after Ernest Lawrence, who invented the cyclotron, a machine that speeds up particles and helped scientists create many new elements.

name: Rutherfordium
summary: Rutherfordium is a radioactive artificial element made by smashing lighter atoms together in particle accelerators. Only small numbers of atoms have ever existed, and they break down too quickly for any practical use.
fact: Rutherfordium is named after Ernest Rutherford, the New Zealand-born physicist who discovered that atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus.

name: Dubnium
summary: Dubnium is a highly radioactive artificial element created in particle accelerators. So few atoms have been made that scientists must study its chemistry one atom at a time before it decays.
fact: Dubnium is named after Dubna, the Russian town that is home to a famous laboratory where many superheavy elements were first made.

name: Seaborgium
summary: Seaborgium is a radioactive artificial element that sits below tungsten in the periodic table. It can only be made a few atoms at a time, and experiments suggest it behaves chemically much like tungsten.
fact: Seaborgium is named after the American chemist Glenn Seaborg, who was still alive when the name was officially approved, a very rare honor.

name: Bohrium
summary: Bohrium is a highly radioactive artificial element made by fusing lighter atoms together in particle accelerators. Only a few atoms exist at a time, and they decay quickly, so it has no uses beyond research.
fact: Bohrium is named after Niels Bohr, the Danish physicist whose model of the atom placed electrons in fixed energy levels around the nucleus.

name: Hassium
summary: Hassium is a radioactive artificial element that sits below osmium in the periodic table. Scientists have made only small numbers of atoms, yet they showed it forms an oxide that evaporates easily, just as osmium does.
fact: Hassium is named after Hassia, the Latin name for the German state of Hesse, where it was first made at a laboratory in Darmstadt.

name: Meitnerium
summary: Meitnerium is a highly radioactive artificial element first made in Germany. Its atoms last only a short time, so very little is known about its chemistry and it has no practical uses.
fact: Meitnerium is named after Lise Meitner, the Austrian-born physicist who helped explain nuclear fission but was overlooked for the Nobel Prize.

name: Darmstadtium
summary: Darmstadtium is a highly radioactive artificial element that sits below platinum in the periodic table. Only a few atoms have been made, and they decay so quickly that its properties are mostly predicted rather than measured.
fact: Darmstadtium is named after Darmstadt, the German city whose research center first created it by firing nickel atoms at a lead target.

name: Roentgenium
summary: Roentgenium is a highly radioactive artificial element in the same column as copper, silver, and gold. Scientists have produced only a few atoms, so no one knows what a solid piece would look like.
fact: Roentgenium is named after Wilhelm Roentgen, the German physicist who discovered X-rays and won the very first Nobel Prize in Physics.

name: Copernicium
summary: Copernicium is a highly radioactive artificial element that sits below mercury in the periodic table. Experiments on single atoms suggest it is unusually volatile, meaning it would turn into a gas very easily.
fact: Copernicium is named after Nicolaus Copernicus, the astronomer who argued that Earth orbits the Sun rather than the other way around.

name: Nihonium
summary: Nihonium is a highly radioactive artificial element whose discovery is credited to scientists in Japan. Its atoms survive only briefly, so it has no practical uses and is studied to test ideas about superheavy atoms.
fact: Nihonium takes its name from Nihon, a Japanese word for Japan that is often translated as land of the rising sun.

name: Flerovium
summary: Flerovium is a highly radioactive artificial element that sits below lead in the periodic table. Only a small number of atoms have been made, and each one decays very quickly after it forms.
fact: Flerovium is named after the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions in Dubna, Russia, which itself honors the physicist Georgy Flerov.

name: Moscovium
summary: Moscovium is a highly radioactive artificial element made by firing calcium atoms at americium. Its atoms typically last for less than a second, so it exists only briefly inside research laboratories.
fact: Moscovium is named after the Moscow region of Russia, which includes the town of Dubna, where the laboratory that helped discover it is located.

name: Livermorium
summary: Livermorium is a highly radioactive artificial element that sits below polonium in the periodic table. Only a small number of atoms have ever been made, and they fall apart in a fraction of a second.
fact: Livermorium is named after the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California, whose scientists worked with Russian researchers to discover it.

name: Tennessine
summary: Tennessine is a highly radioactive artificial element in the same column as fluorine, chlorine, and iodine. It is one of the most recently discovered elements, and only a small number of atoms have been made.
fact: Tennessine is named after the American state of Tennessee, home to Oak Ridge National Laboratory, which supplied material needed to make it.

name: Oganesson
summary: Oganesson is a highly radioactive artificial element with the highest atomic number of any element made so far. It sits in the noble gas column, but scientists predict it may not behave like a typical noble gas.
fact: Oganesson is named after Yuri Oganessian, a Russian physicist of Armenian descent, who was still living when the element officially received his name.
